problem: Embodied AI simulators assume one agent alone in a static home. Prior human-aware simulators either (a) move humanoids as rigid bodies on rails (iGibson 2.0), (b) cover few scenes (SEAN: 3), (c) have no robots (VirtualHome), or (d) are an order of magnitude slower. As a result, no fast, realistic platform existed for training and evaluating robots that collaborate with humans, including evaluation with real humans in the loop.
motivation: Assistive robots must share space with people who change the environment. Testing on hardware with real humans is unsafe, costly, hard to scale and hard to standardize. Simulation can replace it only if humanoids are realistic and diverse and the simulator stays fast enough for RL, which needs hundreds of millions of steps.
key_idea: Build a Habitat simulator in which SMPL-X humanoids are made cheap by caching (precomputed body shapes and blend shapes, cyclic AMASS walk clips, VPoser reach poses looked up by hand position). Add a client-server human-in-the-loop (HITL) tool, and lift navigation and rearrangement into two human-robot collaborative benchmarks, Social Navigation (find and follow) and Social Rearrangement, with RL and heuristic baselines.
insight: Caching humanoid shape, skin and motion keeps a humanoid+robot pair almost as fast as two robots (136±8 vs 150±13 FPS in a single env; 1191±3 FPS over 16 envs on one GPU), so RL with humanoids is practical. Sensor ablations for Social Nav separate two phases. Removing humanoid GPS hurts finding the most (S 0.97→0.76, SPS 0.65→0.34). Removing arm depth hurts following the most (F 0.44→0.19, CR 0.51→0.71). In Social Rearrangement, partner diversity trades in-distribution performance for zero-shot coordination: Learn-Single goes 98.50→50.94 SR from train-pop to ZSC-pop, while Plan-Pop3 goes 77.79→71.79. Swapping oracle skills for learned skills under a frozen high-level policy collapses train-pop SR to 41.09. Removing the primitive move/turn actions raises SR but more than doubles collisions (train-pop CR 0.12→0.32). The HITL study with 30 people preserves the automated ordering (Learn-Single has higher RE, Plan-Pop3 higher RC), so automated humanoid evaluation is a reasonable proxy for relative ranking.
method: Humanoid appearance: SMPL-X body model, rendered as an articulated skeleton with rotational joints (used for physics and collision) plus a linear-blend-skinned mesh (visuals only). 12 cached base bodies (4 male, 4 female, 4 neutral) with precomputed rig and blend shapes; pose-dependent deformation is dropped for speed.

Humanoid motion/behavior: hierarchical. A planner or policy calls low-level skills. Navigation follows path-planner waypoints: rotate to face the next waypoint, then walk forward playing a single-cycle AMASS walk clip cyclically. Pick/place interpolates VPoser reach poses precomputed offline and indexed by 3D hand position, then kinematically attaches or detaches the object.

HITL infrastructure: client-server design. The server runs simulation, agent inference and avatar control; the client handles only rendering and input (mouse/keyboard, browser, VR). Episodes can be recorded and replayed at several abstraction levels and re-rendered from other cameras.

Social Navigation task + baseline: a Spot robot must find and follow a humanoid walking between random points at 1-2 m. Metrics are finding success S, SPS (vs an oracle that knows the humanoid's trajectory), following rate F and collision rate CR. The baseline is an end-to-end DD-PPO policy (ResNet-18 + 2-layer LSTM, ~8.5M params) from arm depth, a binary humanoid detector and humanoid GPS to continuous linear/angular velocity. The reward shapes distance (1-2 m band), orientation, +10 success and -0.1 slack.

Social Rearrangement task + baselines: robot and humanoid move 2 objects (known start/goal 3D coordinates) in unseen HSSD homes. A two-layer policy is used: a learned high-level RL policy picks discrete skill/object combos plus 4 primitive move/turn actions. Low-level skills are oracle (GT-map navigation, instantaneous pick/place) or learned (DD-PPO nav/pick/place). Baselines differ only in the training partner population: Learn-Single (jointly learned single humanoid), Plan-Pop_p (1-4 planner-driven partners), Learn-Pop (8 randomly initialized learned humanoids).

Evaluation protocols: train-pop-eval (known partners, unseen scenes) vs ZSC-pop-eval, a 10-partner zero-shot population (3 Learn-Single checkpoints, 3 Learn-Pop checkpoints, 4 planner agents). Metrics are SR and Relative Efficiency RE vs the humanoid alone. A HITL user study (30 participants, latin-square ordering) fits a GLMM on task steps.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 visual encoder + 2-layer LSTM policies trained from scratch with DD-PPO (social-nav policy; high-level rearrangement policy over oracle or learned low-level skills); plus a non-learned heuristic expert baseline
setting.model_size: ~8.5M params (8517k for nav policies, 8540k for pick/place skills)
setting.training_data: HSSD-200 subset in Habitat 3.0: 37 train scenes × 1000 episodes (12 val scenes × 100 eps, 10 test scenes × 15 eps), YCB objects. Social nav ~200M env steps (~4 days on 4 A100). Rearrangement high-level policy 100M steps with oracle skills. Learned nav/pick/place skills 300M/100M/50M steps. Humanoid partners are scripted planners or jointly RL-trained policies.
setting.observation: Spot arm depth camera (224×171, hFOV 55) + binary humanoid detector + humanoid GPS (relative distance/heading) for social nav. For rearrangement: 256×256 depth, proprioception (arm joints, base egomotion), humanoid relative position, and object start/goal 3D coordinates.
setting.action_space: Social nav: continuous 2-D linear/angular base velocity. Rearrangement: discrete high-level selection of skill+object/receptacle plus 4 primitive forward/backward/turn actions. Learned low-level skills output base velocity + 7-D delta arm joint angles + grasp snap.
setting.simulator: Habitat 3.0 (HSSD scenes, Boston Dynamics Spot robot, SMPL-X humanoids)
setting.privileged: Humanoid GPS (relative position of the humanoid) is given at all times. Rearrangement main results use oracle low-level skills (GT map for navigation, instantaneous pick/place) and GT object start/goal coordinates. The Heuristic Expert social-nav baseline uses the GT environment map.

numbers_note: The paper does not state whether the automated evaluations use the val (12 scenes × 100 eps) or test (10 scenes × 15 eps) split; 'test' is assumed. Only the HITL study explicitly uses test scenes. Social-nav S/SPS/F/CR/BYR and rearrangement/HITL CR were printed as fractions and are converted to 0-100 here; RC (ratio of objects rearranged by the robot) is kept as printed; TD/FD are in meters. ± values (std over 3 seeds) are omitted. The learned-skills row has inconsistencies: the main table gives 41.09±21.5 / RE 79.62 / ZSC SR 21.44±18.16, the appendix table gives 41.09±2.15 / 79.63 / 21.44±18.26, and the text says '77.79% → 41.96%'. An extra '- Primitive actions' ablation (Plan-Pop_3 without move/turn actions) reaches train-pop SR 85.71 / RE 124.36 / CR 0.32 and ZSC SR 76.80 / RE 111.97 / CR 0.33; it is not listed as a separate entry. Per-ZSC-partner breakdowns and simulator FPS benchmarks (scene size, number of agents) appear only in figures. Headline FPS numbers are in the text: robot 245±19, humanoid 188±2, robot-robot 150±13, robot-humanoid 136±8, and 1191±3 over 16 envs.
results: Humanoid+robot simulation runs at 1191±3 FPS across 16 environments on one GPU, close to two robots. The paper says it is an order of magnitude faster than other humanoid simulators. On Social Navigation, the map-free end-to-end RL policy reaches S 0.97, SPS 0.65, F 0.44, CR 0.51, versus the privileged-map Heuristic Expert at 1.00 / 0.97 / 0.51 / 0.52; the RL policy learns emergent backing up and yielding. On Social Rearrangement, Plan-Pop_3/4 generalize best to unseen partners (ZSC SR 71.79 / 71.32) while Learn-Single overfits (98.50 → 50.94). With 30 real humans, both Learn-Single (RE 133.80) and Plan-Pop_3 (RE 123.46) make people significantly faster than working alone (solo TS 1253.17), preserving the automated ranking.
limitations: Humanoid motion is limited to walking and reaching, built from interpolated static poses. It shows artifacts when rotating in place and uses fixed LBS with no pose-dependent skinning. It cannot yet do complex motions such as opening cabinets or sitting.

Rearrangement assumes GT start/goal object coordinates, open receptacles and no communication. Main results use oracle skills; the high-level policy trained on them collapses with learned skills (SR 77.79 → 41.09).

HITL participants observe differently from simulated humanoids. The ZSC humanoid population does not capture how reactive real humans are (every HITL episode succeeded), and social-nav humanoids just follow shortest paths to random points.
